Needs an EU-established entity (EUR 2,000 to 10,000 to form) before the first sale.

SVC3-E9: A logistics-provider blog says the responsible person assumes real legal liability; another vendor page does not say whether liability transfers. Liability and the cost of insurance are unverified and could make a bootstrapped entrant uninsurable.

v6_provisional.note: Provisional: scores judged by the researcher from agent_reported evidence; the entrant-edge hard gate caps them. This is NOT a v6 rank.

entrant_edge.statement: Under 19 CFR 111.1, refunds and drawback for others are customs business, and for IEEPA only the importer of record or the licensed broker that filed the entries can file a CAPE declaration, so a licensed broker holds the legal right to file for third parties. But the licence is open to any US citizen who passes an 80-question exam, importers can self-file for free, the IEEPA right sits with the broker that filed the entries (not the entrant), and incumbents such as GingerControl (15 to 30 percent) and large law firms with contingency offers already operate.

alternatives.label: CBP CAPE self-filing in ACE for IEEPA refunds (entry numbers in a CSV, no fee mentioned on the page; IEEPA only, not drawback)
Carrier or broker auto-filing and pass-through of IEEPA refunds where the carrier was importer of record (DHL Express)
Drawback service providers on contingency at 15-30 percent of recovered amounts (22.5 percent of $10,000 recovered a month shown)
In-house drawback filing in ACE by the importer (described as possible but rarely matching a specialist's recovery)

metadata.cheapest_alternative: CBP CAPE self-filing in ACE for IEEPA refunds (entry numbers in a CSV, no fee mentioned on the page; IEEPA only, not drawback)

economics.note: Illustrative assumptions: 10 clients recovering $60,000 a year each at a 20 percent fee gives $120,000; tooling, errors-and-omissions and filing costs about $15,000. Pessimistic (fee x0.8 = 16 percent, 5 clients, cost x1.5) gives about $48,000 less $22,500 = $25,500 on paper, but this ignores claim rejections, unpaid contingency and a 330-day path to first revenue, so it is treated as failing.

kill_reasons.reason: For IEEPA refunds the free CAPE portal needs only entry numbers and carriers such as DHL file automatically; only the importer of record or the filing broker may file, so an outside recovery firm cannot file.
Drawback is already sold by specialists on 15 to 30 percent contingency and by large law firms for IEEPA; a licensed-broker entrant has no exclusive right, because importers may file for themselves.
The IEEPA refund wave is temporary and the entrant needs a customs broker licence (80-question exam, US citizen) before it can file for others, which pushes first revenue to roughly 11 months.

legal_notes: SVC4-E4: 19 CFR 111.1 defines customs business to include refunds, rebates and drawback of duties, so doing this for others generally requires a customs broker licence (or the importer filing itself); exceptions were not researched and are unverified.

SVC4-E3: for IEEPA refunds only the importer of record or the licensed broker that filed the entries can file a CAPE declaration, and attorneys cannot file for importers per CohnReznick; this blocks an unrelated third-party recovery firm.

SVC4-E7: the broker exam requires US citizenship, age 18 and a score of 75 percent on 80 questions; exam fee, licence application and filer-code steps were not verified, and a licensed individual is needed for a corporate broker.
